Open amateur radio software, built to work together. QSO Graph is open amateur radio software for your station: logging, nets, awards, spots and your radio, in one place, on Windows, macOS and Linux, with the libraries and AI integrations behind them. They share one data model, publish their interfaces, and are built so that any of them can be used alone. Free software under the GPL, for individual operators and for clubs, small and large.

22 MCP servers (156 tools) connect AI assistants to the services hams use every day. Ask your assistant to look up a callsign, check your LoTW confirmations, find POTA spots, or get a band-by-band propagation forecast, all in plain language. The servers: logbooks (QRZ, LoTW, eQSL, HamQTH), public services (POTA, SOTA, IOTA, space weather, WSPR, OMISS), ADIF, propagation analytics, N1MM Logger+ and NetLogger Getting Started: install uv, then add a server to your MCP client Security: credentials stay in your OS keyring, never in files, logs or what the AI sees

ADIF is the base. Every QSO Graph tool reads and writes ADIF, the format the whole hobby already shares, and uses ADIF's own definition for every field ADIF defines. No one-off custom fields: when a tool genuinely needs something ADIF doesn't have, it is defined once, published, and used the same way across every QSO Graph tool where it applies. That costs more than a quick private field, and it's a cost accepted deliberately: it's what keeps the tools working together, and what lets you take your log anywhere. Every tool stands alone, and the pieces talk through published interfaces and shared reference data, not shared code. The rules behind that are in the QSO Graph specification, being rewritten for QSO Graph Desktop.

QSO Graph's Python tools run with uv. There's nothing to install per server: your MCP client runs each one with uvx, always the current release. # Install uv once (Linux / macOS; see Getting Started for Windows) curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh # Try any server uvx pota-mcp # Command-line tools: credentials, and the local-LLM relay uv tool install qso-graph-auth uv tool install qsp-client See Getting Started for MCP client configuration.

QSO Graph is open amateur radio software for your station: logging, nets, awards, spots and your radio, in one place, on Windows, macOS and Linux, with the libraries and AI integrations behind them. Each tool does one job and stands alone; together they share ADIF and published interfaces, so an operator or a club can use the one that applies and add others later. It started with the MCP servers, which let an AI assistant answer questions from an operator's own data: "Do I have any new LoTW confirmations?" "What's the solar forecast?" "What POTA spots are on 20m right now?" The products page lists what is available and what is coming.

A QSO is a radio contact between two stations. Graph refers to the network of connections between operators, bands, modes, and propagation paths. QSO Graph is the connective tissue between ham radio services and the tools operators actually use.

Greg Beam, KI7MT — Advanced class amateur radio operator, software engineer, and builder of the IONIS-AI HF propagation prediction system. 49,000+ QSOs across all HF bands. Based in Idaho. QSO Graph grew out of the IONIS-AI project's need to integrate with ham radio services for validation and analysis. Every QSO Graph tool is useful on its own: you don't need IONIS-AI to use QSO Graph.

IONIS-AI — Ionospheric Neural Inference System. Physics-constrained neural network for HF propagation prediction, trained on 14 billion amateur radio observations. ionis-mcp — MCP server for propagation analytics using IONIS-AI datasets (175M+ signatures from WSPR, RBN, contests, and PSK Reporter). ionis-jupyter — Jupyter notebooks for propagation research. qso-graph-auth — OS keyring credential management for all authenticated QSO Graph servers. adif-mcp — ADIF 3.1.8 spec engine — validation, parsing, enumerations, geospatial.

The Amateur Data Interchange Format is the foundation of amateur radio logging interoperability. adif-mcp includes ADIF's published specification files, unmodified, for the previous and current versions (3.1.7 and 3.1.8), as ADIF publishes them for reuse. Author: Joe Turley, G3ZOD (R.G. Turley OBE) Website: adif.org.uk Test corpus: CreateADIFTestFiles by G3ZOD — 6,191 records exercising every enumeration value

These packages serve facts from each owner's published list, credited to the owner. The owner's document is not included: each package links to it and records its SHA-256 so anyone can check the facts against it. Our GPL-3.0-or-later license covers our code, not their data.

QSO Graph servers wrap external APIs — we don't replicate them. Every server implements rate limiting, response caching, and graceful degradation to be respectful consumers of these services. If a service goes down, we back off. We never retry in tight loops. These services are run by volunteers, non-profits, and small organisations who serve the amateur radio community. We are guests in their house.

To every operator who uploads a QSO, every beacon that transmits, every skimmer that decodes, and every volunteer who keeps these services running — thank you. QSO Graph is a thin layer on top of decades of community effort. 73 de KI7MT

A desktop home for your station. Your callsigns, your logins for the services hams use, and the places you operate from, kept safely in one place, with Parks On the Air, the sun and the moon, band conditions and ADIF's definitions a click away. Free software, on Windows, Linux and macOS, and everything you enter stays on your computer.

Releases page → No account is needed. Open the newest numbered release (QSO Graph Desktop 0.x.y), scroll to its Assets, and take the file for your computer: Computer File Then Windows …-win-x64.exe Run it. From 0.2.0 the installer is signed by Gregory Beam (KI7MT). The signature is new, so Edge may say the file isn't commonly downloaded (choose Keep), and Windows may say it protected your PC: More info shows Publisher: Gregory Beam, then Run anyway. Each platform also has a portable .zip, and SHA256SUMS.txt lets you check any download. The application checks for updates once a day (Release or Beta, or off, in Settings) and never restarts without asking. The install page has the details.

Anyone can copy this project and publish a build of their own. An official download proves it is one, three ways. If it doesn't verify, it isn't an official build. Who published it. Windows: right-click the .exe → Properties → Digital Signatures. It says Gregory Beam. Linux: a package from our repository is checked by apt or dnf against our signing key, E4EC 9751 F1AA 66AB 2BA5 08EF 0410 96B9 A6EB D256. A file from the Releases page is covered by the next two checks. macOS: in Terminal, spctl -a -vv "/Applications/QSO Graph Desktop.app" says accepted, Notarized Developer ID, Developer ID Application: Greg Beam. That it wasn't changed. Its SHA-256 matches the release's SHA256SUMS.txt: on Windows, certutil -hashfile <file> SHA256; on Linux, sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS.txt --ignore-missing; on macOS, shasum -a 256 <file>. Where it came from. GitHub signs, in a public log, that each file was built by this repository's CI from a named commit. Nobody can make that for this repository, a copy of it included. With GitHub's gh: gh attestation verify <file> -R qso-graph/qso-graph-desktop. Every one is on the attestations page. Releases, Betas and Dailies. A Release (0.6.0) is for everyone. A Beta (0.6.0-beta.1) is the next release before it is final, offered in the app to those who choose Beta in Settings. A Daily (Daily build of 0.6.0) is the day's build of main, on the Releases page for 7 days and never offered by the app: for trying what is coming, not for running your station. docs/RELEASES.md explains them.

Keep your callsigns and their logins for QRZ.com, QRZ Logbook, Logbook of The World, eQSL, HamQTH and Club Log, in your computer's own credential store: Credential Manager on Windows, the keyring on Linux, Keychain on macOS. Passwords are never shown again and never leave the computer. Keep your Locations: grid, DXCC, zones, county and ARRL section the way LoTW wants them, and your POTA, SOTA, WWFF and IOTA references. Start one from a park or a summit in a click. Parks On the Air: the parks near you, even with no internet; who is on the air from a park right now; and the parks in your area that have been activated least. Astro: sunrise, sunset, twilight, the moon, and the gray line on a world map. Conditions: solar flux, the K and A indices, NOAA's space weather and a band-by-band outlook. ADIF Lookup: every ADIF field and list value, in ADIF's own words. Back up and restore your callsigns and Locations, and run it portable from a USB stick. The User Guide walks through each, and CHANGELOG.md says what is new in each release.

There is no account to make and no server of ours. Your callsigns, Locations, settings and logs stay on your computer, and your logins stay in its credential store. The application goes online only for what you ask of it, such as reference data, a page of outside data, or the daily update check, and sends nothing about you. PRIVACY.md says exactly what it does. Every connection goes through the application's own core, over HTTPS, using AWS-LC's FIPS-validated cryptographic module on Windows and Linux. The windows and the extensions open no connection of their own, and nothing listens for one. SECURITY.md says how to report a security problem.

Everything past callsigns and Locations is an extension, built on the same extension API anyone can build on, and you choose which ones run: each starts off until you turn it on. The core gives every extension your identities without ever showing it a password, verified reference data, its own storage, and one look and way of working, so an extension author writes only the ham part. Today the application loads its own official extensions; extensions by other authors arrive once the sandbox they run in is finished. Want to write one? See CONTRIBUTING.md.
You need the Node version in .node-version, Rust, CMake and Go. Then make setup and make start. CONTRIBUTING.md has the rest: building, testing, the specification and how changes are made.

QSO Graph Trust signs and uploads your QSOs to ARRL's Logbook of The World (LoTW). It's a security-hardened library and command-line tool written in Rust: your key stays in your computer's credential store, every file it reads is tested against millions of broken and malicious files, and no key data is left in memory it frees. It's part of the QSO Graph Project, and a ground-up rewrite, not a method-by-method port of TQSL. What it does was decided from the sources below, and how it does it is its own.

Your key stays in your computer's credential store, leaving it only to sign or into a backup QSO Graph Trust encrypts itself. QSO Graph Trust is built to the standard of enterprise security software, and every point below is a test or a check that runs on every change: OS credential stores only: the macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager or the Secret Service on Linux. Never a key file, and never a password or passphrase needed on the command line. Nothing it writes holds your key or a password, and no key data is left in memory it frees. A custody test searches every file, output, log and the program's own memory to prove it. Every file it reads is tested against millions of broken and malicious files (fuzz testing), and every length and count is capped, so a bad file is refused rather than crashing it. Memory-safe Rust: no unsafe code in the library, the command line or anything that parses a file. The one exception is the small binding to AWS-LC, the cryptography library, which is also the only C or C++; policy checks enforce both. Only LoTW, only HTTPS, only ARRL's roots, with the server's certificate always checked. A locked supply chain: pinned dependencies, policy checks and CodeQL on every pull request, and signed, notarized and attested releases. Nothing merges until it passes: over 450 tests, over 2.5 million broken and malicious test files, eight security policy checks, a search of memory and every file written for any trace of a key, and GitHub's CodeQL code scanning, on every change. How each is tested, and how to report a security problem privately: SECURITY.md.

ARRL's LoTW developer documentation: developer information, the signed log, .tq8, submitting QSOs, LoTW's PKI, certificate security, station locations, TQSL's command line, and the LoTW Trusted Partners guidelines. TrustedQSL: its source at v2.8.7, read for what LoTW receives; tqsllib's API documentation; and TQSL's change log. QSO Graph Trust carries two things of TQSL's, both ARRL's, under ARRL's terms: the TQSL configuration (config.xml), from which its LoTW tables are generated, and ARRL's root and CA certificates (the 2015 pair as TQSL embeds them, the 2023 pair as ARRL issues them in a .tq6). TQSL 2.8.7, built from its own source, is the reference its signed records and signatures are tested against, byte for byte. Other open-source projects: rfrht's qso-web, credited below, and a survey of 126 ham-radio Rust crates on crates.io, which found no other LoTW signing crate. Standards: ADIF 3.1.8; RFC 5280 (X.509 certificates), RFC 4055 and RFC 8017 (RSA), RFC 1952 (gzip); W3C XML 1.0.

Hams who want to sign and upload their QSOs to LoTW from the command line or their logger, with their key in their computer's credential store. Authors of loggers and tools, who want LoTW signing inside their own program, through the library or the qg-trust command line.

qg-trust signs your ADIF (.adi or .adx) or Cabrillo log with your LoTW callsign certificate and uploads it to LoTW, in one command. It brings over everything you have in TQSL from a TQSL backup: certificates, keys, station locations and the record of what you have already signed. It also requests and renews certificates and manages station locations. Loggers that run tqsl can run qg-trust with the same options, exit codes and final status line.

Your key stays locked away. It lives in your computer's own credential store (the macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager, or the Secret Service on Linux), never as a file someone could copy, and leaves it only to sign. Every QSO is checked by ARRL's own rules before it's signed. A QSO LoTW would refuse is named, with the reason, and the rest are signed. Signatures are byte for byte what TQSL makes. It works inside the program you already use. Another logger or a script can sign and upload for LoTW directly, and the library puts signing inside your own program. It's signed. The macOS program is signed by QSO Graph and notarized by Apple, the Windows program is signed by QSO Graph, and the Linux packages and their repositories are signed with QSO Graph's release key.

macOS (Apple silicon) and Linux, with Homebrew: brew install qso-graph/tap/qso-graph-trust Debian, Ubuntu: sudo curl -fsSL -o /usr/share/keyrings/qso-graph.gpg https://packages.qso-graph.net/qso-graph.gpg echo "deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/qso-graph.gpg] https://packages.qso-graph.net/apt stable main" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/qso-graph.list sudo apt update && sudo apt install qso-graph-trust Fedora, RHEL, Rocky: sudo curl -fsSL -o /etc/yum.repos.d/qso-graph.repo https://packages.qso-graph.net/qso-graph.repo sudo dnf install qso-graph-trust Windows: download qg-trust-<version>-windows-x86_64.zip from the latest release and put qg-trust.exe on your PATH. Every release also has the macOS and Linux programs, and SHA256SUMS.txt to check them against. With Rust: cargo install qso-graph-trust-cli.

qg-trust import ~/tqsl-backup.tbk # certificates, keys, locations and your signing record qg-trust cert list # what you have, and when each certificate expires qg-trust send mylog.adi -l Home # sign mylog.adi for station location Home and upload it A key that TQSL protected with a password is asked for once, when you import it, with what you type hidden. send leaves out QSOs you signed before unless you ask, and keeps mylog.tq8 beside the log. qg-trust sign mylog.adi -l Home signs without uploading; qg-trust upload mylog.tq8 uploads it later. To sign only some dates, add -b 2026-01-01 and -e 2026-06-30. When ARRL starts issuing under a new root, its .tq6 brings the root, and qg-trust import names it with its SHA-256 fingerprint before trusting it: run it again with --trust-root <fingerprint> once you know it is ARRL's. A new root in your own TQSL backup is trusted and named. qg-trust root list shows every root your certificates chain to, and qg-trust root remove <fingerprint> stops trusting one you accepted. From a logger, the tqsl options work as they are: qg-trust -x -d -l "Home" -a compliant -u mylog.adi qg-trust --help lists everything, and the command line's page has every command, option and exit code.

Use qg-trust sign contest.log -l Home to sign a Cabrillo log with your saved station location. QG Trust recognizes the format from the file contents. It accepts Cabrillo 2.0 and 3.0 and skips X-QSO records. If QG Trust refuses the log, the message gives the physical line number and the requirement to meet. Open the original log in a text editor, correct that line, and run the command again. The message contains no calls or values copied from your log. Requirement Correction START-OF-LOG must be 2.0 or 3.0 Export a supported Cabrillo version or correct the version header. Header text must be UTF-8 Save or export the file with UTF-8 encoding. CONTEST must contain 1 to 32 ASCII letters, digits, or hyphens Use the contest sponsor's identifier. Remove internal spaces and other punctuation. QSO mode must be one of CW, PH, FM, RY, DG Correct the mode code using the contest's Cabrillo format. Received exchange must have exactly one call candidate Correct the exchange layout or export ADIF with an explicit CALL field. No single received-call field fits every QSO Correct the exchanges on the two QSO lines named in the message, or export ADIF. A contest identifier outside ADIF 3.1.8's Contest_ID list is accepted when its syntax is valid and the same single received-call field fits every QSO. Missing or ambiguous received calls refuse the whole log before signing. QG Trust follows the format rules even when another reader accepts the file.

Compare your TQSL locations with the QG Trust store: qg-trust location tqsl Each location is new, the same, different, or refused. A different location shows both values for each changed field. Fix a refused location in TQSL, then run the command again. Use --json for machine-readable output. Add selected new locations by name, or add all new locations: qg-trust location tqsl --add Home --add Portable qg-trust location tqsl --all Locations already in the store are never overwritten. By default, the command uses TQSLDIR when it is set and nonempty. Otherwise, it uses %APPDATA%\TrustedQSL on Windows and $HOME/.tqsl on other systems. If TQSL uses a different folder, give its path with --folder. For example, on macOS: qg-trust location tqsl --folder "$HOME/Library/Application Support/TrustedQSL"

QG Interop gives radio app developers Rust and C libraries for specification events and commands, and gives operators the qg-interop listener, capture decoder, and simulator. The library implements QGI-SPEC-001 0.1.0 for all 17 WSJT-X message types, schemas 1–3, N1MM Logger+ XML, fldigi XML-RPC, and QGI event carriage over UDP and TCP. Events preserve native evidence and distinguish observations from commands. Applications supply observer context and own transport and control policy.

Its events describe heartbeats, radio state, decodes, logged QSOs, and shutdown messages. Each observation includes the complete native datagram. Decode one captured native message from a file or standard input: qg-interop decode --wsjtx capture.bin qg-interop decode --wsjtx - < capture.bin Listen to N1MM Logger+ broadcasts on 127.0.0.1:12060 with qg-interop listen --n1mm, or decode a captured XML datagram with qg-interop decode --n1mm capture.xml. See the N1MM guide. Poll local fldigi state and received text as specification NDJSON: qg-interop poll --fldigi --interval 1000 --count 3 qg-interop decode --fldigi response.xml --request-method rig.get_frequency The poller uses 127.0.0.1:7362 and accepts numeric loopback addresses. See the fldigi guide for setup and library examples. See the event JSON guide. Each command's --help includes examples.

Install with cargo add qso-graph-interop. Default features select wsjtx, n1mm, fldigi, qgi, and serde. Use default-features = false for the core without protocol families or enable conformance to test a third-party codec. The public Codec trait decodes observations, encodes commands from common fields into ordered requests with response metadata, and separately re-encodes native evidence. Typed views expose common fields while preserving the complete event JSON. Stream input uses caller-owned buffers with explicit progress; QGI event carriage has a separate encoding capability. C and C++ applications can use the C ABI as shared or static libraries. Consumers need no Rust toolchain. The ABI also supports Python, .NET, and Node bindings. See the library example, protocol documentation, and contribution guide.

The library forbids unsafe Rust and opens no sockets. The command-line tool accepts numeric addresses and defaults to loopback. Parser, field, context, and event limits are checked before output is published. Shipped dependencies use compatible ranges and committed lockfiles, with cargo-vet, cargo-deny, and cargo-audit checks. See SECURITY.md for private vulnerability reporting.

QG Interop decodes fldigi XML-RPC requests and responses into specification events. It also polls a local fldigi instance for radio state, contact fields, and received text. Install the command-line tool from the checkout: cargo install --path crates/qso-graph-interop-cli --locked

Enable fldigi's XML-RPC server on loopback. Its documented default port is 7362; see --xmlrpc-server-port in doc/fldigi.1.txt of the released 4.2.13 archive. The same release defines DEFAULT_XMLRPC_IP_PORT as 7362 in src/include/data_io.h. qg-interop poll --fldigi qg-interop poll --fldigi 127.0.0.1:7362 --interval 500 --count 3 qg-interop poll --fldigi '[::1]:7362' --count 1 --interval is the delay in milliseconds between complete cycles, from 1 through 86,400,000; it defaults to 1,000. --count counts cycles; zero polls until interrupted. Each cycle queries these methods separately: Method Common observation rig.get_frequency Dial frequency in hertz modem.get_carrier RX audio offset in hertz modem.get_name Native modem name modem.get_submode Native submode main.get_trx_state Transmitting for TX or RX main.get_trx_status Transmitting for tx, tune, or rx log.get_call Contact callsign log.get_locator Contact grid rx.get_data RX text since the preceding query Standard output contains one specification NDJSON event per response, with direction from_application, exchange response, and a distinct correlation_id matching the poll request. The native view identifies the associated method. Faults produce error results. Connection, framing, or codec failures stop polling and go to standard error. The poller sends no setters or transmit commands. Only numeric addresses in IPv4's 127.0.0.0/8 range or IPv6's ::1 are accepted. Names such as localhost are rejected. fldigi XML-RPC uses plain HTTP, so the client restricts it to loopback to keep unencrypted state and RX text off outside networks. Each request has a five-second total timeout, at most 16 KiB of response headers, and a 256 KiB body limit. Chunked replies allow at most 1,024 chunks, with 128-byte chunk lines and 16 KiB of trailers. There are no automatic retries or redirects. RX chunks are separate observations. Multiple clients can consume the same app buffer differently; the codec does not join split characters, deduplicate text, or infer a completed QSO. Callsigns, grids, and timestamps are never parsed from received text.
documents.s: Poll local state and received text

documents.t: Files contain one XML-RPC body. Exclude HTTP headers and transfer framing. Use a request's own method name, or explicitly associate a response: qg-interop decode --fldigi request.xml qg-interop decode --fldigi response.xml --request-method rig.get_frequency qg-interop decode --fldigi response.xml --request-file request.xml qg-interop decode --fldigi --request-method modem.get_name - < response.xml Responses contain no method name. The command-line tool therefore requires --request-method or --request-file for responses, including faults. A request file also supplies byte range arguments for text.get_rx. Capture decoding keeps direction unknown. The library can decode unassociated responses as native evidence; valid faults always map to error results.

Enable the default fldigi feature. Supply one body and caller context through the public codec traits. To associate a response and retain correlation: use qso_graph_interop::{Codec, Context, Direction, Exchange, Text, DecodeOptions, fldigi::{Fldigi, RequestAssociation}}; let mut codec = Fldigi::default(); let options = DecodeOptions::new(Context::new(Direction::FromApplication, Exchange::Response) .with_correlation_id(Text::from("synthetic-Q1AAA-1"))) .with_metadata(RequestAssociation::for_method("rx.get_data")?.into()); let body = b"<methodResponse><params><param><value><base64>Q1EgUTFBQUE=</base64></value></param></params></methodResponse>"; let event = codec.decode(body, &options)?.events.remove(0); assert_eq!(event.value()["fields"]["text"], "CQ Q1AAA"); Use RequestAssociation::from_request_body when you have the original request. It retains the two integer arguments needed to interpret a text.get_rx response. Pass options.verification() to Profile::verify, Codec::reencode, or Event::recognized_with. For authored publication, pass it through PublicationOptions::with_verification to write. Without association, method-dependent verification is unavailable. The structured view never substitutes for caller association. Use Codec::encode_commands to construct an ordered request plan from fields. Each EncodedRequest provides bytes() and response_metadata(). Apply that metadata to the response decode options. Planning does not send requests or imply atomic execution. send_text requires string text and boolean transmit; it returns text.add_tx first, then main.tx only for true. set_frequency requires integer frequency_hz and optionally rx_offset_hz; it returns rig.set_frequency first, then modem.set_carrier if requested. These positive integers are bounded by 2,147,483,647. halt_tx takes no arguments and returns main.abort. Family operations use Annex E's exact arguments. Send each following request only after the preceding request returns its matching success type: double for rig.set_frequency, nil for text.add_tx. Stop on a fault, wrong type, lost association, or transport failure. In particular, an empty-string response is not a nil acknowledgment and must not trigger the next request. Supply separate association and correlation for each request. The sequence has no atomicity, rollback, or retry guarantee. An empty append preserves previously queued text. Appended text does not guarantee on-air content. Command strings reject CR and XML-forbidden characters. Observations preserve original bytes and invalid text. The library opens no sockets and never executes controls; the app owns transport and permission to transmit. See Annex E, protocol evidence, and SECURITY.md for acceptance limits and validation evidence.

Run qg-interop listen --wsjtx to emit one QGI-SPEC-001 0.1.0 JSON event per line. The optional --json flag selects the same output. Read one captured native WSJT-X message with qg-interop decode --wsjtx capture.bin, or use - to read standard input. Each capture contains one complete datagram payload, without transport headers. Every event has spec, family, mapping, kind, context, and fields. WSJT-X observations also have native_version, wire_id, and native. listen receives on a WSJT-X server port, where only WSJT-X instances send, so it supplies direction from_application; decode reads a file whose direction it cannot know, so it supplies unknown. Exchange is unknown in both. Neither infers identity from a sender's network address or wire ID. Skip notices and malformed input diagnostics go to standard error and produce no event. For example, listen reports WSJT-X closing like this: {"spec":"0.1.0","family":"wsjtx","mapping":1,"native_version":"3","kind":"lifecycle","wire_id":"test-instance","context":{"direction":"from_application","exchange":"unknown"},"fields":{"state":"closed"},"native":{"format":"wsjtx_datagram","data":"rbzL2gAAAAMAAAAGAAAADXRlc3QtaW5zdGFuY2U="}} The same datagram through decode has unknown direction, so it is ambiguous with "fields":{"operation":"close"}. qg-interop decode --wsjtx close.bin Common frequencies use integer hertz. WSJT-X clock values use HH:MM:SS.mmm; resolved UTC dates use RFC 3339 with three fractional digits and a final Z. Unresolved or invalid native times leave the corresponding common field absent. Their original bytes remain in native.data. A missing text field is omitted, native null is JSON null, and empty text is "". Invalid text uses {"utf8_bytes":[255]} or {"utf16_units":[55296]} without replacement characters. Finite binary64 values are numbers; nonfinite values use ieee754: and 16 lowercase hexadecimal digits. Consumers must round floating-point numbers correctly. Object member order does not affect equality. fields.radio.instance labels the radio instance carried by the family. It is never an authenticated sender identity. Common fields do not extract callsigns or grids from decode text or parse ADIF. Commands have kind: "control" and omit native evidence. Reading a command never sends it. The library also carries events through qgi: reception appends one via hop with the receiving observer's context while preserving the original event and evidence. Received context and hops remain untrusted. See the protocol reference for validation and limits.
Use qg-interop to turn N1MM Logger+ XML datagrams into specification events for monitoring, captures, and app development.

Configure N1MM Logger+ UDP broadcasts to the listener's numeric IP address and port. Then run: qg-interop listen --n1mm The default is 127.0.0.1:12060. N1MM's External UDP Broadcasts appendix recommends port 12060 for broadcasts and lookup messages. The dated documentation and its hashes are recorded in Annex D. To bind another numeric local address, supply it explicitly: qg-interop listen --n1mm 127.0.0.1:12061 qg-interop listen --n1mm '[::1]:12060' --count 10 Standard output contains one compact specification JSON event per line. Errors and unknown-root skip notices go to standard error. A malformed datagram does not end the listener. --count counts received datagrams, including errors and skips; zero listens indefinitely. As the observer on the broadcast port, the listener supplies direction: "from_application". The exchange remains unknown. The codec preserves that supplied context.

A capture file contains exactly one complete native XML UDP payload. Decode a file or standard input: qg-interop decode --n1mm capture.xml qg-interop decode --n1mm - < capture.xml The decoder supplies unknown direction and exchange because the file does not establish either. UTF-8 and UTF-16 XML are supported. Each observation retains the entire original datagram as base64 in native.data. This evidence includes unknown children and attributes.

Contact additions, replacements, and deletions become qso_logged, qso_changed, and qso_deleted. RadioInfo becomes radio_state, spots become spot, and dynamic results become score. AppInfo and lookup messages use native; lookup timestamps remain available in fields. Frequency and Spectrum inputs become observed control events. Frequencies in common fields are integer hertz. Carried station/radio labels appear in fields.radio; SO2R focus, active radio, running, stereo, and transmitting values stay separate. Cataloged valid timestamps are accepted exactly as sent and represented as UTC instants. Missing or unconvertible values leave their common fields absent. Empty text remains empty, and invalid text uses the specification's raw-code-unit wrapper. A spot's native action determines whether it adds or deletes a spot. A false transmitting value reports N1MM's indication; external PTT or paddles can still transmit. See Annex D's mapping for field meanings. The Rust library can construct set_frequency and n1mm.spectrum commands from fields. Both take integer hertz and emit canonical decimal kHz; Spectrum takes an ordered array of levels and derives the count. Encoding returns bytes to the caller. See the library example.
qg-interop sim generates N1MM contest traffic and plays WSJT-X decodes without a radio or a Python installation. Point it at the numeric address and port where your app listens.
documents.s: Test a receiver with the simulator

documents.t: The built-in synthetic ALL.TXT sample contains 120 decodes in seven cycles. qg-interop sim --wsjtx --to 127.0.0.1:2237 qg-interop sim --wsjtx --to 127.0.0.1:2237 --file ALL.TXT --speed 60 qg-interop sim --wsjtx --to '[::1]:2237' --call Q1ZZZ --grid AA00 --loop Use --from YYMMDD_HHMMSS to start at a timestamp in the log. Playback follows file order, skips transmitted lines, other non-decodes, and modes without an established period. It reports the skipped count and names the modes with missing periods. Both aligned WSJT-X logs and single-spaced logs work. Blank lines and received decodes before --from aren't counted as skipped. Each Decode carries the live cycle time. Speed changes the waiting time while cycle stamps keep their original pace. A gap between logged timestamps doesn't insert empty cycles. Each cycle sends Heartbeat, decoding-start Status, its Decodes, and decoding-end Status. The simulator waits one mode period before the next cycle, including after the last cycle. --speed accepts values greater than zero and at most 1000. --loop starts the log again with continuing cycle times. Stop with Ctrl+C; the simulator sends Clear followed by Close. A termination signal also triggers that sequence. Option Behavior --wsjtx Play ALL.TXT as WSJT-X UDP messages. --to IP:PORT Required numeric IPv4 or IPv6 destination; port 1–65535. Bracket IPv6 addresses. --file PATH Read this local ALL.TXT instead of the embedded sample. --from YYMMDD_HHMMSS Include received decodes at or after this timestamp. --id NAME Instance Id, 1–64 characters; default WSJT-X. --call CALL Status callsign, up to 13 letters, digits, or slashes; converted to uppercase. Default empty. --grid GRID Status Maidenhead locator: two uppercase A–R letters, two digits, optionally two uppercase A–X letters. Default empty. --speed N Scale waiting time; default 1. --loop Repeat playback. A receiver can send Replay back to the simulator's source address and port. Only the configured receiver's exact address and port can issue commands, using the simulator's Id. Replay sends all decodes played so far, marked old, then Status. Clearing Band Activity clears that Replay window. Close requests graceful exit. Changed settings produce Status; there is no separate command acknowledgment. See reaction details and validation.

Test a contest dashboard, logger bridge, or band map without running N1MM Logger+: qg-interop sim --n1mm --to 127.0.0.1:12060 --speed 60 qg-interop sim --n1mm --to '[::1]:12060' --call Q1ZZZ --station SYNTHETIC-02 --radios 2 --rate 240 --speed 60 --seed 42 --count 35 qg-interop sim --n1mm --to 127.0.0.1:12060 --radios 2 --loop Each run starts with AppInfo, radio reports, and a zero score. RadioInfo follows every simulated second and at contact transitions. New contactinfo messages follow the chosen rate. Every fifth contact gets a contactreplace with its previous callsign and timestamp. Every seventh contact gets a contactdelete. Each contact also produces a spot addition and deletion. dynamicresults follows each contact change with the current count and points: two points per contact, three after a replacement, and no points for deleted contacts. The synthetic contest uses points as its total score, with no multipliers. All generated callsigns and station labels are synthetic. Set --call and --station to use your own test identities. With two radios, focus and active radio alternate between 1 and 2 for successive contacts. Radio 1 runs and radio 2 searches and pounces. Only the active radio transmits, and each contact's radionr matches that radio. Initial frequencies are 14.025 MHz and 7.025 MHz, in CW. Option Behavior --n1mm Select the scripted N1MM Logger+ peer. --to IP:PORT Required numeric IPv4 or IPv6 destination, port 1–65535. --call CALL Station and operator callsign, up to 13 ASCII letters, digits, or slashes. Converts to uppercase. Empty or omitted uses N0CALL. --station NAME Computer label, 1–64 printable ASCII characters with a non-space character. Default SYNTHETIC-01. --radios 1|2 One radio by default. Select 2 for single operator, two radio (SO2R) traffic. --rate QSOS_PER_HOUR Integer new-contact rate, 1–3600. Default 120. Edits and deletions don't count toward this rate. --speed N Scale waiting time, with 0 < N ≤ 1000. Default 1. --seed N Unsigned 64-bit seed, 0–18446744073709551615. Default 1. --loop Continue until interrupted, unless --count supplies a limit. --count N Stop after 1–100000 new contacts, including with --loop. Without either option, send 12 new contacts. The logical clock starts at 2026-01-01 00:00:00 UTC. The first contact arrives after 3600 / rate simulated seconds. Timestamps use N1MM's unzoned UTC format, YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS. Radio and contact frequencies use integer 10 Hz units, and spots use decimal kHz. Speed changes only the waiting time. The same seed and options reproduce the same bytes, including timestamps, when incoming commands are the same. Send radio_setfrequency to the simulator's source address and port from the exact configured target address. The selected radio's next scheduled RadioInfo reports the new frequency. Later contacts and spots use that frequency too. Tuning uses 10 Hz resolution, dropping any single-Hz remainder. Spectrum input changes no outgoing traffic. Neither input produces an acknowledgment. This follows the documented QSY and display effects in Annex D's pinned source S1, Setting N1MM's Frequency and Sending Spectrum Data. Ctrl+C or a termination signal stops playback and sends final radio reports with transmission cleared. There is no N1MM Close message. Use N1MM options without WSJT-X or capture selection. See validation and precision policy.

Test an app that controls fldigi without starting fldigi. Start the stand-in in one terminal, then run the poller in another: qg-interop sim --fldigi qg-interop poll --fldigi --count 3 The server uses HTTP/1.1 XML-RPC at 127.0.0.1:7362. Point your controller's fldigi XML-RPC connection at that address. Choose another numeric loopback address when needed: qg-interop sim --fldigi 127.0.0.1:17362 --speed 10 --seed 42 --call Q7ABC --grid EM10 qg-interop poll --fldigi 127.0.0.1:17362 --count 3 --speed scales received text and queued transmission together, from more than zero through 1,000. --seed chooses a reproducible Q-prefixed peer call. --call and --grid customize the synthetic script and initialize the contact call and locator fields. Defaults are Q1AAA, FN31, BPSK31, 14,070,000 Hz, and a 1,500 Hz audio carrier. Changing contact fields through XML-RPC changes their getters; it doesn't rewrite the script. Ctrl+C stops the server. All 50 methods in Annex E's mapping table are served. RF and audio setters return their old values. Modem names and ADIF mode/submode remain distinct. Unknown modem names return No such modem. Unmapped XML-RPC methods receive a fault with code -1 and text <method>: unknown method name. Append text with text.add_tx, then call main.tx. Transmission consumes the queue at an approximate rate for the mode and returns to receive when the queued text finishes. BPSK31 uses about 3.1 bytes per second; BPSK63 and BPSK125 use twice and four times that rate. RTTY uses about 6 bytes per second, CW 2, and MFSK16 3.9. Other modes use an approximate 3 bytes per second unless listed in the implementation policy. The text simulation returns to receive automatically. It produces no audio and uses no rig hardware. Calling main.tx with an empty queue sends no text and waits for text, main.rx, or main.abort. main.rx and main.abort stop consumption; unsent text remains until resumed or cleared with text.clear_tx. main.tune reports tune until stopped. The finite received script accumulates while receiving. text.get_rx_length reports its byte length, and text.get_rx(start, length) reads zero-based byte ranges without consuming them. Use (0, -1) to read all available text. rx.get_data returns bytes since its previous query and drains that separate raw buffer. text.clear_rx clears the visible buffer; it doesn't drain raw data or restart the script. Handle buffer shrinking when maintaining a cursor. The bundled fldigi 4.2.13 server returns an empty string for nominal-nil methods, including text.add_tx, main.tx, and main.abort. The stand-in preserves that response. The codec observes it as native; a client that requires a mapped nil acknowledgment can't advance its multi-request sequence from that reply. The stand-in accepts the ordered requests from Codec::encode_commands so controllers can test the bundled behavior explicitly. For the empty logbook, logbook.last_record returns NONE and logbook.all_records returns the released ADIF header. log.get_band follows rig frequency. Other log fields use fixed synthetic defaults. Received data pauses during transmission or tune. Timing approximates text throughput and doesn't reproduce modem DSP, GUI scheduling, macros, or hardware effects. See source evidence and bounds for malformed requests, transport limits, and range boundaries. Use fldigi options without UDP or capture options.

Capture the native messages with listen or decode, then play each event's native.data: qg-interop listen --wsjtx --count 20 > capture.ndjson qg-interop sim --capture capture.ndjson --to 127.0.0.1:2237 --speed 100 qg-interop sim --capture capture.ndjson --qgi --to 127.0.0.1:2237 Native capture playback sends the recorded bytes unchanged. --qgi instead sends each complete event as one qgi UDP datagram, including carried commands. It doesn't execute those commands. The native UDP transport catalog includes WSJT-X, N1MM, and PSK Reporter IPFIX. TCP and MQTT native captures require their own transport helpers. An optional top-level received_at extension, spelled as YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.mmmZ, supplies receive timing. Adjacent records with timestamps retain their relative delay; a pair missing either timestamp uses a one-second interval. Backward receive times are rejected. Current listen and decode output has no receive-time extension, so it uses that fixed interval. Speed and looping also apply to captures. Capture playback sends only the recorded datagrams; it doesn't append WSJT-X shutdown messages or respond to recorded commands.

ALL.TXT files have a 64 MiB limit, a 16 KiB line limit, and a 100,000-decode limit. The Replay window has a 64 MiB budget and a 100,000-decode limit, including repeated cycles. Reaching a limit exits with an error and sends Clear then Close. Invalid UTF-8 in a log is replaced, as in the Python reader. Numbers outside native field ranges are skipped as invalid lines. Capture files have the same 64 MiB and 100,000-record limits, with at most 1 MiB per NDJSON record and 65,507 bytes per UDP payload. Input validation finishes before opening a sender socket. Confirmed fixed periods are FT8 at 15 seconds, FT4 at 7.5 seconds, and JT4/JT65 at 60 seconds. The recorded FT8_SH label also uses FT8 timing. Q65 plays when its recorded label includes the period and submode, such as Q65-60C. Bare Q65, JT9, MSK144, FST4, and FST4W lack a recorded period setting and are skipped. The simulator does not infer a period from gaps between timestamps. WSPR and Echo have known periods but separate log layouts; they are skipped as non-decodes by the ALL.TXT player. Use native capture playback for WSPRDecode messages. Protocol evidence lists the periods and released sources. A mixed log plays its supported cycles and reports a summary such as 2 lines skipped: Tx, not a decode, or a mode without an established period: JT9, Q65. If nothing playable remains, playback fails with no received decodes and the skipped modes.

--dx-call, --mode, or --frequency selects the original finite nine-message script. Its defaults are N0CALL, FN31, Q1AW, FT8, and 14,074,000 Hz. It includes QSOLogged and runs immediately. Use these options without --file or --capture. qg-interop sim --wsjtx --to 127.0.0.1:2237 --mode FT4 --frequency 7074000
The code QSO Graph's Python packages share, in one place, so it is written and tested once. Standard library only: no dependencies.

Module What qso_graph_lib.adif ADIF's ADI format, read and written as ADIF 3.1.7 defines it. Passes ADIF's own 3.1.7 test files; non-compliant input real logs contain is repaired where it can be and reported in Document.problems, never silently qso_graph_lib.jt.protocol WSJT-X's UDP messages, encoded and decoded: Heartbeat, Status, Decode, WSPRDecode, Clear, Close, Replay and the rest, schema 3, written to WSJT-X's own Network/NetworkMessage.hpp qso_graph_lib.jt.alltxt WSJT-X's ALL.TXT, the log of every decode, read into cycles The JT modules are used by qso-graph-sim and jt-mcp; the ADIF module by the logbook servers and qsp-client.
uv add qso-graph-lib It has no command of its own; it is imported.

from qso_graph_lib.jt import protocol message = protocol.parse(datagram) # ValueError if it isn't a WSJT-X message if message.kind == protocol.MessageType.DECODE: print(message.sender, message.fields["snr"], message.fields["message"]) Unknown message types, and fields past the ones it knows, are ignored, as WSJT-X's protocol requires. A message cut short inside a field it needs is refused. from qso_graph_lib import adif doc = adif.read_file("log.adi") # line ends as written, never text mode for record in doc.records: print(record.fields["CALL"], record.fields.get("BAND")) for problem in doc.problems: # what broke ADIF's rules, and what was done print(problem.offset, problem.message) text = adif.write(records, header={"ADIF_VER": "3.1.7", "PROGRAMID": "my-app"})

ADIF (Amateur Data Interchange Format) is the standard file format amateur radio logging programs use to exchange QSO records. adif-mcp is the specification package of qso-graph: it validates, parses and searches ADIF so an assistant can work with logs safely and accurately. Credentials are handled separately by qso-graph-auth, and each logging service has its own MCP server (see qso-graph.io).
No credentials needed—just install and configure your MCP client.

"Is this ADIF record valid? <CALL:5>KI7MT<QSO_DATE:8>20260928<BAND:3>20m<MODE:3>SSB<EOR>" "What values does the ADIF MODE enumeration allow for digital modes?" "Parse my log file and show me the first 50 QSOs." "How far is it from DN13 to JN48, and what heading should I point the beam?"

adif-mcp ships ADIF 3.1.8 as ADIF publishes it: 186 fields, 25 enumerations and 28 data types. validate_adif_record checks each field against its ADIF data type and, for enumerated fields, against the enumeration: Enumeration values match regardless of case, so LoTW's BAND=15M is accepted as 15m. Import-only values (42 of the Mode enumeration's 91 entries, for example) give a warning, not an error: ADIF allows them on import but not in new records. Compound values such as CREDIT_SUBMITTED (a list of Credit or Credit:Medium entries) are checked entry by entry. SUBMODE must be a valid Submode; one that belongs to a different MODE gives a warning. FT4, for example, is MODE=MFSK with SUBMODE=FT4. Structured types are checked against the grammar ADIF states for them: grid squares (2, 4, 6 or 8 characters, any case) and their extensions and lists (VUCC needs two or four, each four or six characters), Location (XDDD MM.MMM), Boolean (Y or N), and IOTA, WWFF, POTA and SOTA references. What the grammar allows but cannot be right, such as a latitude over 90 degrees or N/S on a longitude, is a warning, never an error. The server also publishes the MCP resource adif://system/version: the service version and the ADIF specification version it serves.
adif-mcp --transport streamable-http --port 8003 Then open the MCP Inspector at http://localhost:8003.

MCP server for EME — Earth-Moon-Earth, moonbounce. When the moon is up from your grid, when it is up from both ends of a schedule at once, what the path costs on 2m, 70cm and 23cm, and which days ahead are least degraded. Part of the qso-graph project. No network, no authentication.

The moon's position is computed here, from the abridged ELP-2000/82 series as Meeus tabulates it (Astronomical Algorithms, chapter 47). That is around 250 lines of standard library and a coefficient table. It is also what WSJT-X does, and the norm for EME software. That matters for more than tidiness. Moonrise and moonset are different for every grid square, so a service-backed answer means a request per location per query — and a planning tool that stalls, rate-limits, or goes dark when a remote service does. JPL Horizons is still here — as the test oracle. Recorded Horizons responses are fixtures, so every CI run checks these numbers against NASA's rather than against themselves. Measured against Horizons for a Boise grid: agreement Azimuth within 0.01° Elevation within 0.003° Range within 9 km of ~392,000 (0.002%) Thirty arcseconds, against a 432 MHz array that is degrees wide.

documents.t: uvx eme-mcp # run it; nothing to install

Tool Description eme_moon_window Moon azimuth, elevation and range from a grid square over time — and, given a second locator, the mutual window when both stations can see it eme_path_loss One-way, round-trip and echo path loss on 2m / 70cm / 23cm, or any frequency eme_degradation How much worse than perigee this moment is, with the moon's declination eme_calendar The least degraded days ahead get_version_info Service version and the ephemeris series used

Sky noise is not included. The full degradation figure an EME operator plans with combines the distance term with the galactic background behind the moon, from the Haslam 408 MHz all-sky map. That map is not yet carried and pinned, so eme_degradation and eme_calendar report the distance term and say so in every answer rather than returning a number that looks complete and is not. Tracked in qso-graph-devel#52. Elevations are geometric: no atmospheric refraction, which lifts an object near the horizon by about half a degree.
documents.s: What this does not yet do

documents.t: They answer different questions and are often confused, so both are returned: echo_db is the one to budget a station with — the radar equation, accounting for the moon reflecting about 6.5% of what reaches it. Near 252 dB on 2m, 262 on 70cm and 271 on 23cm at mean distance, which are the numbers EME operators know. round_trip_db is twice the free-space loss. It ignores the moon entirely.

GPL-3.0-or-later. See LICENSE. The algorithms are from Jean Meeus, Astronomical Algorithms (2nd edition, Willmann-Bell, 1998), chapters 7, 11, 12, 22, 40 and 47 — cited in the source where each is used. The implementation is ours; the mathematics is his and is not claimed.

eQSL uses different date formats across endpoints. eqsl-mcp normalizes everything — you always use YYYY-MM-DD: You provide eqsl-mcp sends Endpoint 2026-03-01 202603010000 DownloadInBox (RcvdSince) 2026-03-01 03/01/2026 VerifyQSO (QSODate)
eQSL requires exact mode matching. SSB won't match USB/LSB. PSK won't match PSK31. Use the exact mode logged by the other station.

AG list cache: the Authenticity Guaranteed member list is cached for 4 hours (eQSL updates it about six times a day), in ~/.cache/eqsl-mcp/ag_members.txt ($XDG_CACHE_HOME if set; %LOCALAPPDATA%\eqsl-mcp\ on Windows). IONIS-AI is an open-source machine learning system for predicting HF (shortwave) radio propagation. Its datasets are curated from the world's largest amateur radio telemetry networks and distributed as SQLite files on SourceForge. ionis-mcp lets an assistant answer propagation questions from them, no SQL required. Source: the IARU's HF Managers Handbook, chapter 9.8, "Definition of ITU-Zones when used by radio amateurs" (IARU Region 1, v8.2; the chapter's pages are dated November 2000). The zone border-lines for amateur use are kept there under IARU Region 1 recommendation REC/99/LH/C4.2; the list was drafted by G3HTA from the ITU's CIRAF zones and approved by all three IARU regions. The 90 ITU zones are the IARU's: this package serves facts from that chapter, each citing its page and zone, and links to the handbook rather than copying it. The tests fetch AD1C's and ARRL's files from their sites to validate the facts; neither is included here. where they differ, the owner's list wins (see docs/TRANSCRIPTION.md). Ask an AI app what WSJT-X is hearing. WSJT-X sends what it is doing and every decode to a UDP Server address; jt-mcp listens there and answers: who is calling CQ, and what kind of CQ (DX, POTA, a contest, a region), who has been heard and how well, what WSJT-X is tuned to, recent decodes and WSPR spots. Read-only, permanently. jt-mcp never sends WSJT-X a message, so it cannot answer a call, key your transmitter or change a setting. No write, no PTT, no transmit control—a permanent constraint, not a first-version limit. The tests assert it against the source. WSJT-X first, and WSJT-X defines the protocol. The UDP message definitions come from the WSJT-X project—Network/NetworkMessage.hpp, at the schema WSJT-X states—because the project that owns a definition is its authority. The code is qso-graph-lib's. Part of the qso-graph project.
uvx jt-mcp # run it; nothing to install

In WSJT-X: File, Settings, Reporting, UDP Server: 127.0.0.1, port 2237 (WSJT-X's defaults). That is all jt-mcp needs when WSJT-X runs on the same PC. Only one program can listen on a UDP port. If GridTracker, JTAlert or another logger already listens on 2237, give jt-mcp a different port (--udp-port) and point WSJT-X at that one.

Tool Answers jt_cq Who is calling CQ, and what kind: plain, DX, activity (POTA, SOTA, WWFF, IOTA), contest (TEST, FD, RU, WW), region (NA, EU, ...), or a frequency (CQ 290). The latest per station jt_status What each WSJT-X is doing: dial frequency and band, mode, DX call and grid, Tx enabled or transmitting, your call and grid jt_decodes Recent decodes, each read into its parts (who is calling whom, grid, report, sign-off); filter by callsign, CQ only, SNR, band jt_heard Stations heard: how often, last SNR, last grid, mode and band jt_wspr WSPR spots WSJT-X decoded: call, grid, power, SNR, drift jt_diagnostics The listener: where it listens, who may send, what arrived, what was dropped and from where, each WSJT-X's version get_version_info Service version and status Times are UTC. Several WSJT-X instances (two radios, two bands) are kept apart by the Id each sends, such as WSJT-X - FT-991A.

By default jt-mcp listens on 127.0.0.1, this PC alone. For WSJT-X on another PC, give one address of this PC with --bind, and name each PC that may send with --allow: "args": ["jt-mcp", "--bind", "192.168.1.50", "--allow", "192.168.1.40"] and set WSJT-X's UDP Server to 192.168.1.50. Listening on every interface at once (0.0.0.0) is refused, --allow is required with a network address, and names are not accepted, only IP addresses. A datagram from anyone else is dropped unread and counted, and jt_diagnostics shows the count and the addresses. What the allow list does not do. It keeps other machines out. It is not proof of who sent: a UDP sender's address can be forged by anything on the same network. What contains that is that jt-mcp only reads, so a forged datagram can mislead about what WSJT-X is doing and cannot make anything happen.

Meteor scatter planning for amateur radio: can these two stations work each other on this shower, and when. That is the whole shape of it. Meteor scatter is a point-to-point mode, so a radiant elevation on its own tells an operator nothing they can act on — the question is always about a path between two stations. Part of the qso-graph project.

Three things, and radiant elevation is only one of them. 1. Path length. Trails burn at about 85–120 km, so a single-hop reflection off something that low works from roughly 400 km to about 2300 km. Shorter and the reflection point would have to be nearly overhead, where there is very little qualifying sky; longer and it sits below both horizons. 800–2000 km is where the geometry is best, and it is what hams actually run. 2. Radiant elevation at the path midpoint — not at either station. The reflection happens near the middle, so that is the sky that matters. Below the horizon there are no trails to reflect from. Very high is also poor, because trails then run down the path rather than across it. 3. The angle between the radiant and the path. This is the one usually left out, and it is the one that decides whether a reflection is geometrically possible at all. A trail reflects specularly only where it is tangent to the ellipsoid with both stations at its foci. Trails running along the path can never be tangent to it; trails running across it can. So a radiant broadside to the path is good and a radiant up- or down-path is poor — at the very same elevation. All three are reported, and the verdict says which one decided it.

Because the physics above is a tangency condition, and what a station actually hears also depends on its power, its antenna and the sporadic background. A figure like "73" would imply a precision none of that supports. So the answer is no / marginal / good / best, each with the reason beside it.

documents.t: Shower radiants, numbers and names are the IAU Meteor Data Center's — the body that names and numbers meteor showers. The package carries the facts read from the MDC's Established showers file with its URL and SHA-256 recorded, so the exact edition served is identifiable. The MDC is maintained on an unpaid voluntary basis and asks to be cited; its requested references are returned by meteor_source_info, printed in NOTICE, and travel inside every answer that uses a radiant. The MDC lists several published solutions per shower, each from a different study. All of them are kept and none is blended — the average of two published radiants is a third that nobody published and no paper stands behind. Tools return the first-listed solution, labelled, and meteor_shower_info gives them all. Peaks are stored as solar longitude, not as dates, because that is how the catalogue publishes them and it is the right way round: solar longitude names the same point in the stream every year, while a date drifts. This server converts it to the date it falls on in the year you ask about. Two tools read the network, because only those two report what is happening right now: Source Used for Licence Global Meteor Network Confirmed meteor counts today, by shower CC BY 4.0 — attribution is a licence condition, and is returned in the answer NASA CNEOS Recent fireballs US government work Everything else is computed locally and needs no network at all.

meteor_window needs both ends of the path, but you should not have to retype your own. Your end is optional, and a host that knows the operator's station supplies it — in QG Desktop that is the Station component. The fields are ADIF's, not invented here: ADIF field Used for MY_GRIDSQUARE The default grid. ADIF permits 2, 4, 6 or 8 characters MY_GRIDSQUARE_EXT Characters 9–12 of a 10- or 12-character locator MY_LAT / MY_LON An exact position, when the station has one A grid is what hams actually use, so a locator is the normal input here, not a degraded one. It may carry 4, 6 or 8 characters. Operators often state 6 or 8 for their own station, while a structured on-air exchange may carry only 4. Which modes constrain it is not asserted here: ADIF enumerates every mode and submode but says nothing about payload length, so there is no authority to infer precision from mode — 4 is the safe floor for all of them. A grid square is a rectangle, though, and its centre is all a locator gives. Nothing here assumes a precision: the slack is computed from the characters each locator actually carried. At 4 characters that is about ±100 km per end, so a path length carries about ±200 km of slack; at 6 it falls to a few km. That is immaterial on a 1100 km path and decisive against a threshold — a path reported as 2250 km could be 2050 to 2450, which straddles the 2300 km single-hop limit. When a limit falls inside that slack the answer says the call cannot be decided at on-air precision, and what would settle it. The slack is reported either way. So MY_LAT/MY_LON are used when a station has them, and the answer always says which it used and how precisely each end was located. A 2-character MY_GRIDSQUARE is a legitimate ADIF value but is refused for a path: a Maidenhead field is 10 by 20 degrees, around 1100 km across, which is wider than the entire usable meteor-scatter range. The refusal explains the precision rather than calling the locator invalid, because it isn't.
documents.s: Your own end comes from your station profile

documents.t: ADIF's location fields describe the transmitting station, not where the operator is sitting — MY_LAT is "the logging station's latitude". That is what makes a remote operation come out right without a special case: the reflection geometry depends on where the antenna is. ADIF separates the three callsigns for exactly this reason — STATION_CALLSIGN (used over the air), OPERATOR (the person), and OWNER_CALLSIGN ("the callsign of the OPERATOR's host"). So operating a remote station in FN42 from a chair in DN13 gives the FN42 path, and the operator's own location never enters the calculation.

N1MM reports transmitting only when it keys the radio itself (macros, its CW keyer), so a paddle or microphone PTT doesn't count as transmit time in n1mm_so2r.

N1MM Logger+ is a Windows contest logger. It can broadcast its state over UDP: contacts, spots, radio info and score. n1mm-mcp listens to those broadcasts and keeps the contest state in memory, so an assistant can answer questions about it. N1MM doesn't know it's there. N1MM Logger+ (Windows) │ UDP broadcast (port 12060, XML) ▼ n1mm-mcp (Python: the same PC, or any OS on the LAN) ├── UDP listener (background) ├── State engine (in memory, per StationName) │ MCP protocol (stdio) ▼ AI assistant

In N1MM: Config → Configure Ports → Broadcast Data, and enable all message types. Set the destination to 127.0.0.1:12060, N1MM's address for "this PC." n1mm-mcp listens there by default, and nothing outside the PC can reach it. N1MM on another PC​ Give one address of this PC and name who may send: n1mm-mcp --bind 192.168.1.20 --allow 192.168.1.40 Then point N1MM at this PC's address (192.168.1.20:12060), or at your subnet's broadcast address (192.168.1.255:12060) to reach every PC on it. N1MM accepts several destinations separated by spaces. Don't use 255.255.255.255: N1MM's own documentation warns that it risks broadcasting to the internet (N1MM: External UDP Broadcasts). --allow is required whenever --bind is a network address, and is repeatable for more than one PC. A datagram from any other address is dropped without being read, and counted — n1mm_diagnostics shows the count and the addresses, so traffic you did not expect is visible rather than silent. --bind 0.0.0.0 is refused. It listened on every interface at once, including whatever Wi-Fi a laptop happened to be joined to, and it cannot be narrowed afterwards. Name the interface you mean. What the allow-list does and does not do​ A UDP sender's address can be forged by anything on the same network, so the list keeps other machines out; it is not proof of who sent a datagram. What limits the damage is that n1mm-mcp only reads: it has no tool that writes to N1MM, your log, or anything else. A forged packet can therefore mislead you about contest state—a wrong frequency, a spot that was never spotted—but it cannot act, and nothing it contains is written anywhere. Treat the state as reported, not as verified, and run on a network you trust.

NetLogger is the logging program many amateur-radio nets use: net control or a logger keeps the check-in list, and anyone can follow the net live. Its server publishes active nets, check-in lists and past nets through a public API.

Every request tells NetLogger which station is asking, so it can tell one user from another: netlogger-mcp/<version> (KI7MT; +https://github.com/qso-graph/netlogger-mcp) The version is the installed one — it is read from the package, not written here. On first use the assistant asks for your callsign and saves it. You're asked once. To set it yourself, use NETLOGGER_MCP_CALLSIGN=KI7MT. It's saved in settings.json, in ~/.config/netlogger-mcp/ (Linux), ~/Library/Application Support/netlogger-mcp/ (macOS) or %APPDATA%\netlogger-mcp\ (Windows).

NetLogger is a donation-funded service on one server, and it limits how often each call may be made. We keep to those limits: Measure Detail NetLogger's call limits GetActiveNets 1/min, GetCheckins 3/min, GetPastNets 1/min, GetPastNetCheckins 10/min. Checked before a request is sent, never after. One budget per user Every copy you run (Claude Desktop, Claude Code, a script) shares one budget, through a locked file beside settings.json. Shared answers Every copy also shares the answers it fetched, so a copy that has hit the limit gets another copy's recent answer, with its age, instead of an error. Response caching Active nets 60 s, check-ins 20 s, past nets 60 s, past check-ins 1 hour. Filtering by name costs no extra calls. How old an answer is Every answer has as_of_utc (when it was given) and age_seconds (how old the data is), so it was fetched at as_of_utc minus age_seconds. Stale answers over errors When a limit is reached, the last answer comes back with its age rather than a new request. 429 back-off A "too many requests" on any call stops all calls for at least a minute, longer if NetLogger asks. Past-net windows More than 7 days of past nets needs a name filter, NetLogger's rule to protect its server. Request timeout 15-second timeout. User-Agent header Every request names this project and your callsign, so NetLogger's operators can see who is asking.

NetLogger's band and frequency are whatever the logger typed ("40M", "75M", "DMR", "7033", "3918 KHz", "147.030 91.5", "TG 3141"). They're returned as typed, and beside them, only when the text can be read reliably: frequency_mhz, band_adif (the ADIF band, from ADIF 3.1.7's Band enumeration), tone_hz and talkgroup. A frequency outside the amateur bands (e.g. GMRS) gets no band_adif.
NetLogger's check-in data includes street addresses and ZIP codes, and past nets include the IP address of whoever opened them. None of these are ever returned.

OMISS is an amateur-radio society that runs SSB nets on HF, from 10 to 160 meters, every day of the week. Members exchange OM numbers on the nets and work toward the society's awards. Its website publishes the net schedule, the member roster, check-in history for every net, and the award rules and recipients.

Net control often opens a net in NetLogger for check-ins well before its listed time (the 40m net has opened 35 minutes early). omiss_net_schedule gives the listed times; omiss_nets_on_air shows whether a net is open now.

Only omiss_nets_on_air needs it: it asks NetLogger, which is told which station is asking. On first use the assistant asks for your callsign and saves it. You're asked once. The other tools don't need it.

omiss.net is a volunteer-run club website, not an API. We read it gently: Measure Detail One request at a time At most one request every 2 seconds, shared by every copy you run (Claude Desktop, Claude Code, a script) through a locked file in your settings folder. Response caching Schedule, officers, Statehood, members and award recipients 24 hours; awards and rules 7 days; history and statistics 1 hour. Stale answers over errors When the site is down or busy, the last answer comes back with its age rather than an error. Back-off A "too many requests" or "unavailable" answer stops all requests for at least a minute, longer if the site asks. Request timeout 20-second timeout. User-Agent header Every request names this project, so the site's operators can see who is asking. NetLogger omiss_nets_on_air keeps to NetLogger's call limits, shared with netlogger-mcp if you run it too.

Every value is checked before it is sent: callsigns, OM numbers, bands from a fixed list, YYYY, YYYY-MM or YYYY-MM-DD dates, numeric net IDs, and award IDs from the site's own list. Free text is never sent to omiss.net. No postal addresses or email addresses are ever returned, even where a page prints one. Members are looked up one at a time, by callsign or OM number. There's no search by state, county or grid, and no roster download.

qrz-mcp uses qso-graph-auth personas for credential management. QRZ has two separate auth mechanisms, exposed as two providers—set up whichever you need: Provider Tools Credentials qrz qrz_lookup, qrz_dxcc username + password qrz_logbook qrz_logbook_status, qrz_logbook_fetch, qrz_download username + API key # Install qso-graph-auth if you haven't uv tool install qso-graph-auth # Create a persona (--start is required) qso-graph-auth persona add --name ki7mt --callsign KI7MT --start 2018-01-01 # XML API (qrz_lookup, qrz_dxcc) qso-graph-auth provider enable ki7mt qrz qso-graph-auth creds set ki7mt qrz # asks for your username, then your password (hidden) # Logbook API (qrz_logbook_status, qrz_logbook_fetch, qrz_download) qso-graph-auth provider enable ki7mt qrz_logbook qso-graph-auth creds set ki7mt qrz_logbook # asks for your username, then your API key # Verify qso-graph-auth creds doctor Pass the persona name (ki7mt above) as the persona argument on every tool call. Omit --password / --api-key to be prompted instead—passing secrets as CLI arguments leaves them in your shell history. XML API (callsign lookup, DXCC) requires a QRZ XML Subscription ($35.95/yr). Free tier returns name and address only. Logbook API requires an API key from QRZ Settings > API.

WSPR beacons transmit a 2-minute encoded signal at very low power (typically 200 mW to 5 W). Each decoded spot proves a propagation path exists between two locations on a specific band. With thousands of beacons worldwide transmitting 24/7, WSPR provides continuous, automated propagation monitoring across all HF bands.

wspr.live is a volunteer-run service that mirrors all wsprnet.org data into a public ClickHouse database. We take our responsibility as a good neighbour seriously: Measure Detail Rate limiting 3 seconds between requests (20 req/min max) Circuit breaker Opens after 3 consecutive failures; exponential backoff up to 5 minutes. Prevents hammering a struggling service. Time-bounded queries Every query filters by time (max 72 hours). No unbounded full-table scans. Band filtering Queries filter by band whenever the user provides one — this hits wspr.live's indexes efficiently. Column selection We SELECT only the columns each tool needs (8-10 per query), never SELECT *. Result limits All queries cap results (200 spots, 50 leaderboard entries). Response caching 2-10 minute TTL per tool. Identical queries within the window hit local cache with zero network traffic. Request timeout 20-second timeout — we don't hold connections open on a shared service. User-Agent header Every request identifies itself as wspr-mcp/{version} so the operators can reach us if needed. If wspr.live is down or overloaded, the circuit breaker backs off automatically. We don't retry in a tight loop.

Security is always our #1 priority. If a feature cannot be implemented safely, it will not be implemented.

Every QSO Graph MCP server guarantees: # Guarantee How It's Verified 1 Credentials never in logs Static analysis + code review 2 Credentials never in tool results All return paths traced 3 Credentials never in error messages All raise/exception statements audited 4 Credentials never in config files OS keyring only (via qso-graph-auth) 5 No command injection surface No subprocess, no shell=True, no os.system 6 No SQL injection surface Parameterized queries or API-only 7 HTTPS only for external calls All URLs audited 8 Rate limiting implemented Prevents user account bans 9 Input validation on all user strings Regex validation before use 10 Fail safely Errors reveal no sensitive information

Credentials flow through the OS keyring and never appear in the MCP protocol: User runs: qso-graph-auth creds set ki7mt qrz ↓ OS Keyring (encrypted by OS) - macOS: Keychain - Windows: Credential Manager - Linux: Secret Service (GNOME Keyring / KWallet) ↓ User asks: "Look up W1AW on QRZ" ↓ AI calls: qrz_lookup(persona="ki7mt", callsign="W1AW") ↓ qrz-mcp: reads credentials from keyring (in-process only) ↓ qrz-mcp: HTTPS request to api.qrz.com ↓ AI sees: {"call": "W1AW", "name": "ARRL", "grid": "FN31pr", ...} ↓ Password NEVER appears in: tool params, tool results, logs, errors
Tool parameters: persona, callsign, band, mode, etc. Tool results: lookup data, QSO records, statistics Error messages: static strings like "Login failed" (never "Login failed with password X")
Passwords API keys Session tokens Any credential values This is enforced by architecture, not policy. Credential values physically do not exist in MCP protocol messages.

All user-provided strings are validated before use: import re CALLSIGN_RE = re.compile(r'^[A-Z0-9]{1,3}[0-9][A-Z0-9]{0,4}(/[A-Z0-9]+)?$', re.IGNORECASE) GRID_RE = re.compile(r'^[A-R]{2}[0-9]{2}([A-X]{2})?$', re.IGNORECASE) DATE_RE = re.compile(r'^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$') BAND_RE = re.compile(r'^\d{1,3}[mM]$') MODE_RE = re.compile(r'^[A-Z0-9]{2,10}$', re.IGNORECASE) Error messages never include the invalid input value — this prevents injection via error reflection.

The following are absolutely forbidden in any QSO Graph server: # FORBIDDEN — Command injection import subprocess os.system(command) subprocess.run(command, shell=True) eval(user_input) exec(user_input) # FORBIDDEN — Credential exposure print(f"Password: {password}") logging.debug(f"API key: {api_key}") raise ValueError(f"Auth failed with password {password}") # FORBIDDEN — Plaintext credential storage with open("config.json") as f: password = json.load(f)["password"]

No package is published to PyPI without completing the full security pipeline: Publishing is gated mechanically, in publish.yml, and every check either passes or the release does not happen. There is no human sign-off step, because a step that depends on somebody being available is not a gate: The run is from main — enforced by the pypi environment's deployment branch rule, not only by the workflow file CI passed on the exact commit being published — the full test suite, ruff, mypy and CodeQL The version agrees everywhere — the typed version, pyproject.toml and server.json must match, and the version must be new on PyPI and untagged tests/test_security.py passes — the credential, HTTPS and injection checks described above pip-audit --strict finds no known vulnerability in the declared dependencies, resolved fresh, and a separate job audits the lockfile weekly Source greps — no subprocess, no plaintext http://, no credential logging The tag is cut last, only after PyPI and the MCP Registry both serve the version, so a green run means published everywhere Earlier versions of this page described an audit request sent to an internal message queue and an independent reviewer returning a PASS. That process was retired: it was not what actually stood between a change and PyPI, and describing a reviewer who does not exist overstates what a reader is getting.

Every server includes automated security tests: No print statements containing credential keywords No logging statements containing credential keywords No subprocess or shell execution All external URLs use HTTPS No credentials in exception messages

The QSO Graph specification is being rewritten for QSO Graph Desktop. The earlier version was written for a separate net logger, a direction QSO Graph has since left. It will be published here again once the rewrite is ready. The rules that every QSO Graph tool already follows still hold: ADIF is the base, ADIF's own definition is used for every field ADIF defines, and credentials stay in your operating system's keyring.

Every package includes test_security.py with 6 source-code audit tests. These scan all Python source files for forbidden patterns — they are not runtime tests. # Test What It Catches S1 test_no_print_credentials print() calls containing password, secret, api_key, or token S2 test_no_logging_credentials logging.*() calls containing credential keywords S3 test_no_subprocess Any use of subprocess or shell=True (command injection) S4 test_all_urls_https Hardcoded http:// URLs (except localhost) S5 test_error_messages_safe Exception messages that could expose credentials S6 test_no_eval_exec Any use of eval() or exec() (code injection) These tests run in CI on every push and must pass before any PyPI publish. If the security gate fails, the publish job is blocked. No exceptions.

adif-mcp is the foundation package. Beyond the standard security and unit tests, it carries a comprehensive validation suite against the ADIF 3.1.8 specification:

The registered validation cases live in the repository, as tests/TEST-CASE-REGISTER.md — each with its input, expected result and the reason it exists. That file is the record; this page used to copy its table and had drifted to a total of 48 against the register's 109, which is what happens to a number kept in two places. Two figures, both measured on 2026-10-28: Registered validation cases 109, all passing Full pytest suite 186 tests — the registered cases plus unit, security, CLI and packaging tests

The gold standard for ADIF validation: the official test files from G3ZOD's CreateADIFTestFiles, which exercise every enumeration value in the specification. Both the current and previous versions are run, because logs written against 3.1.7 do not stop existing when 3.1.8 publishes: Corpus QSO records ADIF 3.1.8 6,202 ADIF 3.1.7 6,197 Test Records Result Zero false errors on all official records (3.1.8) 6,202 PASS — 0 errors All warnings are correct behavior (3.1.7) 6,197 PASS — 37 warnings (21 user-defined fields + 16 import-only values) Enum JSON files match official exports 25 files PASS — all identical Rule: If our validator rejects an official ADIF test record, our validator is wrong.
