Publishing is gated mechanically rather than socially. publish.yml checks that CI passed on the exact commit being published, that the version agrees across pyproject.toml and server.json and is new on PyPI and untagged, that tests/test_security.py passes, that pip-audit --strict reports no known vulnerability, and that no subprocess, plaintext http:// or credential logging appears in src/. The tag is cut last, only after PyPI and the MCP Registry both serve the version. This page previously described three rounds of human review — a writer and two independent audit/reviewers — as a requirement before any publication. That was retired. It was not what stood between a change and PyPI, and describing reviewers who are not there overstates what a reader is getting.

The build kit for QSO Graph's applications: the tools it takes to compile and package them, installed with one command, at pinned versions. Part of the qso-graph family of amateur-radio tools; sister to JTSDK (WSJT-X) and FLSDK (fldigi). Choose what you work on, and get exactly its tools. Each kind of work is a profile: Profile For Installs desktop QSO Graph Desktop, the Electron hub Node.js, Rust, and Go and CMake for its FIPS crypto module; on Windows also Ninja, NASM, libclang, Perl and git logger QSO Graph Logger, the Qt application Qt, its compiler, CMake, Ninja; NSIS on Windows for the installer mcp qso-graph's MCP servers uv, and the Pythons the servers test against (3.11 to 3.13); git on Windows Install one or several; run the installer again with another profile to add it. Why it exists. A program nobody else can build is a program nobody else can keep alive. QGSDK writes down, as code, everything it takes to build an application, so a new maintainer starts from one command instead of from someone's memory. QGSDK is the tooling; an application is compiled and packaged from its own checkout, with these tools.

Version Windows Linux macOS For logger Qt 6.12.0 MinGW build GCC build universal build (Apple silicon and Intel) the framework the logger is written in Compiler MinGW 13.1.0, Qt's own, matched to Qt's libraries the system's GCC Apple's clang (Xcode command-line tools) CMake 3.30.5 ✓ ✓ ✓ configures and builds; CPack makes the packages Ninja 1.12.1 ✓ ✓ ✓ runs the build NSIS 3.13 ✓ the Windows installer desktop Node.js 26.9.0 ✓ ✓ ✓ the application, and its build Rust 1.99.1 ✓ ✓ ✓ the credential core; installed with rustup, inside the prefix Go 1.27.3 ✓ ✓ ✓ building AWS-LC's FIPS module CMake 4.4.4 ✓ ✓ ✓ building AWS-LC's FIPS module Ninja, NASM 1.13.2, 3.02 ✓ building AWS-LC's FIPS module on Windows libclang 23.1.4 ✓ bindgen, which the FIPS module needs on Windows (only libclang and its headers are unpacked) Perl 5.42.3.1 ✓ the FIPS module's build on Windows (Strawberry Perl's portable build; only perl\ is unpacked) C/C++ compiler Microsoft's C++ Build Tools (needs an administrator) the system's GCC Apple's clang (Xcode command-line tools) git MinGit 2.56.0.4 the system's the Xcode command-line tools' mcp uv 0.13.6 ✓ ✓ ✓ the servers' environments, tests and builds Python 3.11 to 3.13 ✓ ✓ ✓ installed by uv, inside the prefix git MinGit 2.56.0.4 the system's the Xcode command-line tools' every profile Python 3.14.10 ✓ ✓ ✓ QGSDK's own scripts only; never part of an application What QGSDK can't install without root or admin rights comes from the system, and the installer checks for it first: on Windows Microsoft's C++ Build Tools (desktop); on Linux a C++ compiler and the libraries Qt uses (logger), a C/C++ compiler, make, unzip and libatomic (desktop), and git (desktop, mcp); on macOS Apple's Xcode command-line tools (every profile). It names what's missing, with the one command that installs it. Linux arm64 (a Raspberry Pi 5) has the desktop and mcp profiles; Qt's Linux build, and so the logger, is x86-64 only. Every version is pinned, and every download checked, in manifest.json: the one place to change them.

You need nothing installed first: no Python, no git, no Visual Studio, no Qt account, no admin rights. The one exception is the desktop profile: Rust on Windows links with Microsoft's C++ Build Tools, which only Microsoft's installer can install, as an administrator. The installer checks and, if they're missing, prints the one command: winget install Microsoft.VisualStudio.2022.BuildTools --override "--quiet --wait --add Microsoft.VisualStudio.Workload.VCTools --includeRecommended" Get QGSDK: download the latest release's .zip from Releases, check it (Verify your download) and unpack it; or clone this repository. Install the tools for your profiles (once; the logger is about 2 GB and a few minutes): powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File bootstrap\install.ps1 -Profiles desktop,mcp Leave out -Profiles and it asks. Everything goes into .\prefix beside this checkout. Running it again installs only what's missing or changed. Removing QGSDK is deleting the folder. Load the tools into your shell, whenever you open a new one: . .\prefix\qgsdk-env.ps1 # PowerShell prefix\qgsdk-env.cmd # cmd Work in the application's checkout: QSO Graph Desktop with npm (its README); the logger with CMake; an MCP server with uv. Keep QSO Graph Desktop's checkout near the top of a drive (C:\src\qso-graph-desktop, say): Microsoft's compiler can't open a path longer than 260 characters, and the credential core's build folders nest deep. qgsdk doctor shows what's installed and where; qgsdk profiles lists the profiles. qgsdk build --source <logger checkout> is a shortcut for the logger's configure-and-build step; you never need it.

Tested on Rocky Linux 9, Debian 12 and Ubuntu 24.04; any x86-64 distribution of that age or newer should work, and arm64 for the desktop and mcp profiles. Install what your profiles need from your distribution (the one step that needs root). For every profile: # Fedora / RHEL / Rocky / Alma sudo dnf install gcc-c++ mesa-libGL-devel mesa-libEGL-devel libxkbcommon-devel tar dbus-libs fontconfig freetype libbrotli glib2 libwayland-cursor libxkbcommon-x11 xcb-util xcb-util-cursor xcb-util-image xcb-util-keysyms xcb-util-renderutil xcb-util-wm git gcc make unzip libatomic # Debian / Ubuntu sudo apt install g++ libgl-dev libegl-dev libxkbcommon-dev curl tar libdbus-1-3 libfontconfig1 libfreetype6 libglib2.0-0 libwayland-cursor0 libxkbcommon-x11-0 libxcb-cursor0 libxcb-icccm4 libxcb-image0 libxcb-keysyms1 libxcb-render-util0 libxcb-render0 libxcb-shape0 libxcb-util1 libxcb-xkb1 git build-essential unzip libatomic1 The desktop profile alone needs a C/C++ compiler, make, git, unzip and libatomic (build-essential git unzip libatomic1 on Debian); the mcp profile alone needs only git, curl and tar. The installer checks for everything its profiles need and prints the line for you if anything is missing. Get QGSDK: download the latest release's .tar.gz from Releases, check it (Verify your download) and unpack it; or clone this repository. Install the tools for your profiles (once; the logger is about 2 GB, under a minute on a fast line). No root: bootstrap/install.sh --profile desktop --profile mcp Load the tools into your shell, whenever you open a new one: . ./prefix/qgsdk-env.sh Work in the application's checkout, as on Windows.

macOS 14 or newer, Apple silicon or Intel. Install Apple's Xcode command-line tools, if you haven't (the one step that needs an administrator): xcode-select --install Get QGSDK: download the latest release's .tar.gz from Releases, check it (Verify your download) and unpack it; or clone this repository. Everything goes into ./prefix; running it again installs only what's missing or changed. Load the tools into your shell, whenever you open a new one: . ./prefix/qgsdk-env.sh Work in the application's checkout, as on Windows.

Each release carries SHA256SUMS, and GitHub's signed record that this repository's Release workflow made every file. In the folder you downloaded to: (Get-FileHash qgsdk-0.1.2.zip -Algorithm SHA256).Hash # Windows: compare with SHA256SUMS sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS --ignore-missing # Linux shasum -a 256 -c SHA256SUMS --ignore-missing # macOS With the GitHub CLI, on any platform, this checks who made it: gh attestation verify qgsdk-0.1.2.zip -R qso-graph/qso-graph-sdk

On a clean machine (a fresh VM or container is best): powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File tests\windows-check.ps1 # Windows tests/check.sh # Linux and macOS Each installs QGSDK from nothing with every profile (or those named with -Profiles / --profile). For the logger it builds a small Qt program, builds it again with plain CMake, and runs both (on Windows it also checks NSIS runs); for mcp it runs each of the servers' Pythons through uv, and git, and checks they are the prefix's; for desktop it clones QSO Graph Desktop, checks the Node.js and Rust it pins are the ones installed, and runs its setup, build and fast check. It ends with == PASS or == FAIL: <what>. CI runs them on Windows, Linux (x86-64 and arm64) and both kinds of Mac whenever the installer changes, and weekly, so a moved download, or a QSO Graph Desktop pin QGSDK doesn't match, is found within a week.

QSP—relay MCP tools to any OpenAI-compatible local LLM endpoint. Named after the Q-signal QSP ("Will you relay?"), qsp-client relays tool calls between a local LLM and MCP servers. It is an MCP client: any model with function calling gains access to the qso-graph servers' tools, from local weights, not from cloud. Formerly qsp-mcp. See Moving from qsp-mcp.
uv tool install qsp-client # the qsp-client command, on your PATH uv add qsp-client # or into your own project

# Interactive mode qsp-client --config ~/.config/qsp-client/config.json # Single query qsp-client --query "What bands are open from DN13 to JN48 right now?" # Direct endpoint (no config file needed if no MCP servers configured) qsp-client --endpoint http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions --api-key sk-xxx

The config format is Claude Desktop compatible—copy your existing mcpServers block directly: { "mcpServers": { "ionis": { "command": "ionis-mcp", "env": { "IONIS_DATA_DIR": "/path/to/datasets/v1.0" } }, "solar": { "command": "solar-mcp" }, "wspr": { "command": "wspr-mcp" } }, "bridge": { "endpoint": "http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions", "model": "AstroSage-70B", "temperature": 0.3, "system_prompt": "You are an expert ham radio operator and RF engineer.", "max_tool_calls_per_turn": 5, "profiles": { "contest": { "servers": ["n1mm", "ionis", "solar", "wspr"], "temperature": 0.2, "system_prompt": "You are a contest advisor. Be concise." }, "propagation": { "servers": ["ionis", "solar", "wspr"], "temperature": 0.3 }, "full": { "servers": "*", "temperature": 0.3 } }, "server_timeouts": { "ionis": 1, "solar": 8, "qrz": 5 } } } The mcpServers block uses the exact same format as Claude Desktop. The bridge section is qsp-client specific (ignored by Claude Desktop).

qsp-client [OPTIONS] Options: -c, --config PATH Config file path (default: ~/.config/qsp-client/config.json) -e, --endpoint URL LLM endpoint URL (overrides config) -k, --api-key KEY API key for the LLM endpoint -m, --model NAME Model name (overrides config) -p, --profile NAME Tool profile (contest, dx, propagation, full) -q, --query TEXT Single query mode — ask one question and exit --enable-writes Enable write-capable tools (disabled by default) --list-tools List available tools and exit --version Show version
Command Action /tools List available tools /help Show help quit Exit (also: exit, q, 73)

qsp-adif-convert converts an ADIF (.adi) log to JSON or NDJSON, with filters for band, mode, callsign, date range and confirmed QSOs: qsp-adif-convert -i mylog.adi -o mylog.json qsp-adif-convert --help It works on files on your own machine and opens no connection. It used to be adif-mcp convert; adif-mcp is now only the MCP server.

qsp-client is a strict, stateless pipe between an LLM and MCP tools: No caching, no shared state, no health polling All state lives in MCP servers All inference optimization lives in the inference server (prefix caching, KV-cache) qsp-client just connects the two sides Works with any OpenAI-compatible endpoint: llama.cpp, Ollama, vLLM, SGLang.

Write-capable tools disabled by default (--enable-writes opt-in) Credentials stay inside MCP servers (OS keyring)—never exposed to qsp-client or the LLM No subprocess, no shell execution, no eval All external connections HTTPS only (LAN endpoints exempted)

qsp-client is qsp-mcp, renamed: in the MCP world, -mcp names mark servers, and this is a client. Install the new name: uv tool uninstall qsp-mcp && uv tool install qsp-client. Your config keeps working: ~/.config/qsp-mcp/config.json and ~/.qsp-mcp.json are still read, after the new ~/.config/qsp-client/config.json and ~/.qsp-client.json. The qsp-mcp command still works, and says it has moved. Use qsp-client.
